tagline: Alpine peaks, four languages, one country
overview:
Switzerland is a small, landlocked country wrapped around the middle of the Alps, hemmed in by France, Germany, Austria, Italy and Liechtenstein. It covers about 41,000 km², roughly twice the size of New Jersey, and mountains take up more than half of it. About 9 million people live there, most in the flatter belt between the Alps and the Jura hills where Zurich, Geneva, Basel and the capital, Bern, sit.

Switzerland has four national languages: Swiss German in the center and east, French in the west, Italian in the south, and Romansh, kept alive by a small community in the southeast. It is a federal republic of 26 cantons that run much of their own affairs, and Swiss voters decide national questions directly in referendums held several times a year. The country has stayed neutral in wars since 1815, which is why Geneva hosts the Red Cross and many United Nations agencies. Chocolate, cheese, watches and banking are its best-known industries.
landAndNature: The Alps curve across southern Switzerland with dozens of peaks above 4,000 meters, including the pyramid-shaped Matterhorn and Dufourspitze, the highest at 4,634 meters. Glaciers such as the Aletsch, the largest in the Alps, grind slowly down the valleys, though they are shrinking as the climate warms. Their meltwater feeds rivers that leave the country in every direction, including the Rhine and the Rhône, so Switzerland is often called Europe's water tower. Lakes Geneva, Constance and Lucerne fill deep basins carved by ice. Ibex, chamois, marmots and golden eagles live on the high slopes, and lynx and wolves have returned to the forests.
peopleAndCulture: Swiss life is shaped by mountains and by punctuality: trains run to the minute, and cable cars climb to villages with no roads at all. Cheese is serious business, from holey Emmental to Gruyère melted into fondue and scraped hot as raclette, and Swiss makers invented milk chocolate and the machine that grinds it smooth. Alphorns, yodeling and cattle parades down from summer pastures mark mountain traditions, while Fasnacht carnival fills Basel's streets with masks and drums for three days. Skiing, snowboarding, hiking and ice hockey fill the calendar, and citizens vote on national questions up to four times a year.
history: Celtic Helvetii tribes gave Switzerland the Latin name still stamped on its coins. In 1291 three forest communities swore an alliance in the mountains, a founding pact remembered every August 1, the national day. Swiss soldiers became Europe's most feared mercenaries before the country turned away from foreign wars. Reformation preachers such as Zwingli and Calvin split the cantons along religious lines in the 1500s. After a short civil war in 1847, Switzerland adopted a federal constitution in 1848 that still stands, among the oldest in the world. It stayed neutral through both world wars, hosted the founding of the Red Cross in 1863, and granted women the vote in national elections in 1971.
funFacts: Switzerland has four national languages, and Romansh is spoken by fewer than 50,000 people in one mountain region.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel, 57 kilometers long, is the world's longest railway tunnel, bored deep beneath the Alps.
Milk chocolate was invented in Switzerland in 1875, and conching, the process that makes chocolate smooth, followed soon after.
Swiss voters go to the polls several times a year to settle national questions themselves, more often than any other country.
Swiss coins carry the Latin word Helvetia, chosen so that no one of the country's four languages is favored.
